cards.body: Write the 2x2 matrix equation relating (lambda1, y1) to (lambda2, y2) and note that det\((S) = 1\). Matrix equation 1 · coordinates & determinant 1.

cards.q: If the reference planes \( RP_1 \) and \( RP_2 \) are conjugate (object and image) planes, then in \( y_2 = c y_1 - d \lambda_1 \) the element \( d \) must be ____.
cards.why: When \(d = 0\), \(y2 = c y1\) is independent of the initial ray angle \(\lambda1\), and c is the lateral magnification.

cards.q: When \( d = 0 \) between conjugate object and image planes, the matrix element \( c \) equals the ____.
cards.why: With \(d = 0\), \(y2 = c \cdot y1\), so \(c = y2 / y1 = m\).

cards.q: In the system matrix \( S = \begin{bmatrix} b & -a \\ -d & c \end{bmatrix} \), the element \( a \) is the ____.
cards.why: A parallel incident ray \((\lambda1 = 0)\) emerges with slope \(\lambda2 = -a y1 = -(1/f) y1\).

sheets.title: Q13 · Interference by division of wavefront and division of amplitude (2 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 13
cards.q: State the principle behind the interference obtained by division of wave front and amplitude methods.
Principles and examples of both division of wavefront and division of amplitude

options.t: Both wavefront division (narrow source, spatially split wavefront, e.g. Young/biprism) and amplitude division (extended source, partial reflection/transmission, e.g. thin film/Michelson) explained

cards.why: Explain how coherent beams are derived from a single source in both classes.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Division of wavefront vs division of amplitude
cards.body: Know first: Interference: division of wavefront. In division of wavefront, a primary wavefront from a narrow slit or point source is spatially divided into two coherent beams by apertures, mirrors, or prisms (e.g., Young's double slit, Fresnel's biprism, Lloyd's mirror). In division of amplitude, the amplitude (intensity) of an incident beam (usually from an extended source) is divided into two coherent beams by partial reflection and transmission at a boundary (e.g., thin films, Newton's rings, Michelson interferometer).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Comparison of the two interference classes
cards.tex: \text{1. Division of wavefront: } S \to (S_1, S_2) \text{ spatially (point/slit source)} \\ \text{2. Division of amplitude: } E_{\text{inc}} \to E_{\text{refl}} + E_{\text{trans}} \text{ at boundary (extended source)}
cards.body: State the principle and an example for division of wavefront and division of amplitude. Division of wavefront 1 · division of amplitude 1.

cards.q: Fresnel's biprism and Fresnel's double mirror produce interference by division of ____.
cards.why: They split two spatial halves of the cylindrical wavefront from a narrow slit.

cards.q: Newton's rings and the Michelson interferometer produce interference by division of ____.
cards.why: Each ray is split into reflected and transmitted amplitudes at a partially reflecting surface.

cards.q: A broad extended source can be used to produce bright fringes in interference by division of ____.
cards.why: In amplitude division, each ray interferes only with its own reflected/transmitted partner.

sheets.title: Q14 · Definition of numerical aperture for optical fiber (2 marks)
sheets.source: PYQ Nov 2020 Q14 · also Nov 2019 Q2

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 14
cards.q: Define numerical aperture for optical fiber.
Sine of maximum acceptance angle and formula NA = \(\sqrt{n1^2 - n2^2}\)

options.t: Defined as sine of maximum acceptance angle (measure of light-gathering power) and formula NA = \(\sin \theta_a = \sqrt{n1^2 - n2^2}\) given
Only formula or only verbal definition given

cards.why: Define NA as \(\sin(\theta_a)\) and write its expression in terms of n1 and n2.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Numerical aperture (NA) of an optical fiber
cards.body: Know first: Laws of reflection and refraction from Fermat's principle. The numerical aperture (NA) of an optical fiber is defined as the sine of the maximum acceptance angle \( \theta_a \) at which light incident on the fiber core from air is guided by total internal reflection: \( \text{NA} = n_0\sin\theta_a = \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2} \approx n_1\sqrt{2\Delta} \). It measures the light-gathering power of the fiber.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Numerical aperture expressions
cards.body: State the definition of numerical aperture and write the formula in terms of core and cladding indices. Definition 1 · formula 1.

cards.q: The light-gathering power of an optical fiber is directly given by its ____.
cards.why: Light collection efficiency scales as \(NA^2\).

cards.q: For a fiber immersed in a medium of refractive index \( n_0 \), the numerical aperture is \( \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2} \) divided by ____.
cards.why: From \(n0 \sin(\theta_a) = \sqrt{n1^2 - n2^2}\), \(\sin(\theta_a) = \sqrt{n1^2 - n2^2} / n0\).

cards.q: Typical communication-grade silica optical fibers have a numerical aperture in the range ____.
cards.why: Small index difference between core and cladding gives NA ~ 0.14 to 0.29.

sheets.title: Q15 · Explanation of a diffraction grating (2 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 15
cards.q: Explain a diffraction grating.
Periodic N-slit arrangement, grating element \(d = a+b\), and grating equation

options.t: Large number of parallel equidistant slits of width b and spacing a explained with \((a+b) \sin \theta = m \lambda\)

cards.why: Define a diffraction grating and write its grating element and principal maximum equation.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Diffraction grating
cards.body: Know first: N-slit Fraunhofer diffraction pattern and grating (14). A diffraction grating is an optical component consisting of a very large number \( N \) of equidistant, parallel, narrow slits of equal width \( b \) separated by opaque rulings of width \( a \) (typically \( 15,000\text{ lines/inch} \)). The distance \( d = a + b \) is the grating element, and combined single-slit diffraction and multi-slit interference produce sharp principal maxima at \( (a + b)\sin\theta = m\lambda \).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Grating element and principal maxima
cards.tex: d = a + b = \frac{1}{N_0}, \quad d\sin\theta = m\lambda, \quad m = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots
cards.body: Describe the periodic ruling structure and write the grating condition. Description 1 · equation 1.

cards.q: A diffraction grating produces sharp spectral lines by combining single-slit diffraction with ____.
cards.why: Constructive interference of thousands of slits sharpens the principal maxima.

cards.q: To rule a master diffraction grating on an optically flat glass or metal plate, one uses a ____.
options: fine diamond point on a ruling engine
cards.why: A precision diamond ruling engine cuts thousands of parallel grooves per centimeter.

cards.q: For oblique incidence at angle \( i \), the grating equation becomes ____.
cards.why: The total path difference for oblique incidence is \(d(\sin i + \sin \theta)\).

sheets.title: Q17 · Brewster's law and Brewster window (2 marks)
sheets.source: PYQ Nov 2020 Q17 · also Nov 2018 Q12

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 17
cards.q: State Brewster's law and what is Brewster window?
Brewster's law \(\tan \theta_p = n2/n1\) and definition of Brewster window

options.t: Brewster's law (tan theta_p = n2/n1, reflected & refracted rays perpendicular) and Brewster window (zero-reflection loss window for p-polarized light in lasers) explained
Only Brewster's law stated without Brewster window

cards.why: State Brewster's law and explain how a Brewster-angle window transmits p-polarized light with zero reflection.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Brewster's law and Brewster window
cards.body: Know first: Production of linearly polarised light (18). Brewster's law states that when unpolarized light is incident on a dielectric interface at the polarizing (Brewster) angle \( \theta_p \) such that \( \tan\theta_p = n_2/n_1 \), the reflected beam is completely linearly polarized perpendicular to the plane of incidence (s-polarized), and the reflected and refracted rays are mutually perpendicular (\( \theta_p + r = 90^\circ \)). A Brewster window is a plane optical window tilted at \( \theta_p \) (commonly at the ends of a gas laser tube) that transmits p-polarized light with \( 100\% \) efficiency (zero reflection loss), making the laser output linearly polarized.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Derivation of \(\theta_p + r = 90\) degrees
cards.tex: n_1\sin\theta_p = n_2\sin r \quad \text{and} \quad \tan\theta_p = \frac{\sin\theta_p}{\cos\theta_p} = \frac{n_2}{n_1} \\ \implies \cos\theta_p = \sin r = \cos(90^\circ - r) \implies \theta_p + r = 90^\circ
cards.body: State \(\tan(\theta_p) = n2/n1\) and explain that a window set at \(\theta_p\) has zero reflection coefficient for p-polarized light. Brewster's law 1 · Brewster window 1.

cards.q: When light is incident at the Brewster angle \( \theta_p \), the angle between the reflected ray and the refracted ray is ____.
cards.why: Since \(\theta_p + r = 90\) degrees, the reflected and transmitted rays are at right angles.

cards.q: At Brewster's angle of incidence, the reflection coefficient is zero for light whose electric field vector lies ____.
options: perpendicular to the plane of incidence (s-polarized)
cards.why: Oscillating dipoles in the medium cannot radiate along their own axis in the reflected direction.

cards.q: Brewster windows are fitted at the ends of gas laser tubes (such as He-Ne lasers) to obtain a ____.
options: linearly polarized laser beam with zero reflection loss
cards.why: p-polarized light suffers zero reflection loss at each pass, while s-polarized light suffers reflection losses.

sheets.title: Q18 · System matrix for a thick lens (4 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 4 marks
cards.title: Question 18
cards.q: Obtain the system matrix for a thick lens.
Refraction matrices R1, R2 and internal translation matrix T

options.t: R1 = \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -P1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\), T = \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ t/n2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\), and R2 = \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -P2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) written with correct order \(S = R2 T R1\)
Matrices written in wrong multiplication order

cards.why: Write the three elementary 2x2 matrices and set up the product \(S = R2 T R1\).

cards.q: Matrix multiplication to obtain the 2x2 thick-lens system matrix

options.t: Complete 2x2 product S = \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 - P2 t/n2 & -(P1 + P2 - P1 P2 t/n2) \\ t/n2 & 1 - P1 t/n2 \end{pmatrix}\) derived

cards.why: Multiply \(R2 \cdot T \cdot R1\) to obtain the four elements of the thick-lens system matrix.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: System matrix for a thick lens
cards.body: Know first: The thin lens, principal foci and focal length. A thick lens of axial thickness \( t \) and refractive index \( n_2 \) placed in a medium \( n_1 \) consists of refraction at surface 1 (\( P_1 = \frac{n_2 - n_1}{R_1} \)), translation through \( t \) in medium \( n_2 \), and refraction at surface 2 (\( P_2 = \frac{n_1 - n_2}{R_2} \)). Multiplying in reverse order \( S = \mathcal{R}_2 \mathcal{T} \mathcal{R}_1 \) gives \( S = \begin{bmatrix} 1 - \frac{P_2 t}{n_2} & -\left(P_1 + P_2 - \frac{P_1 P_2 t}{n_2}\right) \\ \frac{t}{n_2} & 1 - \frac{P_1 t}{n_2} \end{bmatrix} \).
cards.tex: S = \begin{bmatrix} 1 - \frac{P_2 t}{n_2} & -\left(P_1 + P_2 - \frac{P_1 P_2 t}{n_2}\right) \\ \frac{t}{n_2} & 1 - \frac{P_1 t}{n_2} \end{bmatrix}

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Derivation of \(S = R2 T R1\) for a thick lens
cards.tex: P_1 = \frac{n_2 - n_1}{R_1}, \quad P_2 = \frac{n_1 - n_2}{R_2} \\ \mathcal{R}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -P_1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathcal{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ t/n_2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathcal{R}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -P_2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\ \mathcal{T}\mathcal{R}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -P_1 \\ t/n_2 & 1 - \frac{P_1 t}{n_2} \end{bmatrix} \\ S = \mathcal{R}_2\mathcal{T}\mathcal{R}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -P_2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -P_1 \\ t/n_2 & 1 - \frac{P_1 t}{n_2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 - \frac{P_2 t}{n_2} & -\left(P_1 + P_2 - \frac{P_1 P_2 t}{n_2}\right) \\ \frac{t}{n_2} & 1 - \frac{P_1 t}{n_2} \end{bmatrix}
cards.body: Write the refraction and translation matrices and multiply \(S = R2 \cdot T \cdot R1\). Elementary matrices 2 · matrix multiplication 2.

cards.label: Derivation
cards.title: System matrix of a thick lens, step by step
cards.legend: Thick lens of thickness \(t\) and index \(n\), bounded by spherical surfaces of radii \(R_1\) and \(R_2\). Matrices use the reduced slope \(n\alpha\).

phases.name: First refraction R1
phases.why: air into the lens

phases.name: Internal translation T
phases.why: travel the thickness t in glass

phases.name: Second refraction R2
phases.why: glass back into air

phases.name: Full system product
phases.why: multiply in the order of travel

steps.note: Refraction at the first spherical surface of radius \(R_1\).
Travel the thickness \(t\) inside the glass of index \(n\).

ask.q: What is the off-diagonal entry of the translation matrix \(\mathcal{T}\) inside the lens?
ask.why: With the reduced slope, the height changes by \(t\alpha = t\,(n\alpha)/n\).

steps.note: Refraction at the second surface, from the glass back into air.

ask.q: In what order are the three matrices multiplied for a ray?
ask.why: The matrix of the last element acts on the left, following the ray's travel.

steps.note: With \(P_1 = (n-1)/R_1\) and \(P_2 = (1-n)/R_2\); the \(t\)-term is the thick-lens correction.

ask.q: What does the thick-lens power reduce to when \(t \to 0\)?
ask.why: The thickness term vanishes, leaving the sum of the two surface powers.

steps.note: The equivalent focal length of the thick lens in air.

ask.q: Which part of the lens makes the \(t/n\) term appear?
options: The power of the first surface alone
ask.why: Only the internal translation of thickness \(t\) adds the \(t/n\) term.

cards.q: According to Gullstrand's equation from the thick-lens matrix, the equivalent power \( P \) is ____.
cards.why: The (1,2) element of S is -\(P = -(P1 + P2 - P1 P2 t / n2)\).

cards.q: In the translation matrix for a lens of thickness \( t \) and refractive index \( n_2 \), the reduced thickness is ____.
cards.why: Because \(\lambda = n2 \cdot \alpha\), \(\Delta y = t \cdot \alpha = (t/n2) \cdot \lambda\).

cards.q: A thick lens is formed by two refractions separated by a ____.
cards.why: Between the two curved faces, the ray translates through a homogeneous medium of thickness t.

sheets.title: Q20 · Haidinger's fringes vs Newton's rings (4 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 4 marks
cards.title: Question 20
cards.q: What are conditions for producing Haidinger's fringes? How is it different from Newton's rings?
Conditions for producing Haidinger's fringes

options.t: Extended monochromatic source, plane-parallel film of uniform thickness d (not extremely thin), and telescope focused at infinity

cards.why: State the uniform-thickness film, extended source, and viewing at infinity conditions.

cards.q: Differences between Haidinger's fringes and Newton's rings

options.t: Equal inclination (\(\theta\) varies, \(d\) constant) vs equal thickness (t varies, \(\theta\) constant); localized at infinity vs localized in the film

cards.why: Contrast equal inclination vs equal thickness, localization, and film geometry.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Haidinger's fringes vs Newton's rings
cards.body: Know first: Colours of thin films, Newton's rings, Michelson interferometer (11). Conditions for Haidinger's fringes: (1) a plane-parallel film or plate of uniform thickness \( d \), (2) an extended monochromatic source so rays strike at various inclination angles \( r \), and (3) a telescope (or relaxed eye) focused at infinity to bring parallel reflected rays to a focus. Differences from Newton's rings: Haidinger's fringes are fringes of equal inclination (\( d \) constant, \( r \) varies) localized at infinity (as in a Michelson interferometer), whereas Newton's rings are Fizeau fringes of equal thickness (\( t \) varies radially, \( r \approx 0 \) constant) localized within the wedge-shaped air film and viewed with a microscope.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Comparison of path difference equations
cards.tex: \text{Haidinger fringes (parallel film, } d = \text{const): } \Delta = 2nd\cos r + \frac{\lambda}{2} \; (\text{localized at } \infty) \\ \text{Newton's rings (spherical air wedge, } r \approx 0\text{): } \Delta = 2t(r) + \frac{\lambda}{2} = \frac{r^2}{R} + \frac{\lambda}{2} \; (\text{localized in film})
cards.body: State the three conditions for Haidinger fringes and contrast them with Newton's rings in terms of film geometry, parameter varied, and localization. Conditions 2 · differences 2.

cards.q: Haidinger's fringes are interference fringes of ____.
cards.why: In a uniform plane-parallel plate, each fringe corresponds to a constant inclination angle r.

cards.q: Because rays forming a given Haidinger fringe leave the plane-parallel plate parallel to one another, Haidinger fringes are localized ____.
options: on the surface of the film
cards.why: Parallel rays intersect at infinity (or in the focal plane of a telescope objective).

cards.q: Newton's rings are localized in the air film and are observed using a ____.
cards.why: Fizeau fringes of equal thickness are localized near the thin wedge film.

sheets.title: Q21 · Fraunhofer diffraction at a circular aperture (4 marks)
sheets.source: PYQ Nov 2020 Q21 · also Nov 2022 (D 30197) Q22

cards.label: PYQ · 4 marks
cards.title: Question 21
cards.q: Discuss the intensity distribution caused by Fraunhofer diffraction at a circular aperture.
Airy disc pattern, concentric rings, and angular/linear radius of first minimum

options.t: Central bright Airy disc surrounded by concentric dark and bright rings, intensity curve/formula, and \(\sin \theta1 = 1.22 \lambda / D (r1 = 1.22 f \lambda / D)\) explained
Qualitative description and \(1.22 \lambda / D\) stated without intensity curve

cards.why: Describe the Airy pattern, sketch the intensity distribution, and state the first dark ring condition.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Fraunhofer diffraction at a circular aperture (Airy pattern)
cards.body: Know first: Single-slit Fraunhofer diffraction pattern (12). When plane waves of wavelength \( \lambda \) pass through a circular aperture of diameter \( D = 2a \) and are focused by a lens of focal length \( f \), the diffraction pattern consists of a bright central circular patch (Airy's disc, containing \( 84\% \) of total light energy) surrounded by concentric alternating dark and weak bright rings. The intensity distribution is \( I(\theta) = I_0 \left[\frac{2 J_1(v)}{v}\right]^2 \) with \( v = \frac{\pi D\sin\theta}{\lambda} \), and the first dark ring occurs at \( \sin\theta_1 = \frac{1.22\lambda}{D} \) (linear radius \( R_1 = \frac{1.22 f\lambda}{D} \)).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Airy intensity distribution and ring positions
cards.tex: v = \frac{\pi D\sin\theta}{\lambda}, \quad I(\theta) = I_0\left[\frac{2J_1(v)}{v}\right]^2 \\ \text{Dark rings } (J_1(v) = 0): \quad \sin\theta_1 = \frac{1.22\lambda}{D}, \quad \sin\theta_2 = \frac{2.233\lambda}{D}, \quad \sin\theta_3 = \frac{3.238\lambda}{D} \\ \text{Radius of Airy disc in focal plane: } R_1 = f\theta_1 = \frac{1.22 f\lambda}{D}
cards.body: Explain the circular symmetry of the Airy pattern, write the intensity and dark-ring equations, and sketch the intensity distribution. Pattern & Airy disc 2 · intensity & radii equations 2.

cards.q: Approximately what percentage of the total diffracted light energy is concentrated within the central Airy disc?
cards.why: About 84% of the energy falls inside the first dark ring of the Airy pattern.

cards.q: The mathematical function that describes the amplitude of Fraunhofer diffraction by a circular aperture is the first-order ____.
cards.why: Integrating over a circular aperture yields \(2 J1(v) / v\).

cards.q: Because the objective lens of a telescope acts as a circular aperture, the image of a distant star is a ____.
options: diffraction Airy disc with faint rings
cards.why: Aperture diffraction spreads the point image into an Airy disc of radius \(1.22 f \lambda / D\).

sheets.title: Q23 · Method of producing plane, circularly and elliptically polarized light (4 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 4 marks
cards.title: Question 23
cards.q: Explain the method of producing plane, circularly and elliptically polarized light.
Production of plane (linearly) polarized light

options.t: Passing unpolarized light through a Polaroid or Nicol prism (or reflection at Brewster's angle)

cards.why: Explain how unpolarized light is converted into linearly polarized light.

cards.q: Production of circularly and elliptically polarized light using a quarter-wave plate

options.t: Passing linearly polarized light through a QWP at \(\phi = 45\) deg for circular and \(\phi\) != 0, 45, 90 deg for elliptical polarization
Only circular or only elliptical explained

cards.why: State the orientation of the QWP optic axis relative to the incident linear polarization for both cases.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Production of linear, circular, and elliptical polarization
cards.body: Know first: Production and analysis of polarised light (22). (1) Plane (linearly) polarized light is produced by passing unpolarized light through a Polaroid sheet or Nicol prism (or reflecting at Brewster's angle \( \theta_p = \tan^{-1}n \)). (2) Circularly polarized light is produced by passing linearly polarized light normally through a quarter-wave plate (QWP) with its optic axis inclined at \( \phi = 45^\circ \) to the incident electric vector, giving equal orthogonal amplitudes with a \( \pi/2 \) phase shift. (3) Elliptically polarized light is produced by setting the QWP optic axis at any angle \( \phi \neq 0^\circ, 45^\circ, 90^\circ \), giving unequal orthogonal amplitudes with a \( \pi/2 \) phase shift.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Equations for the three polarization states
cards.tex: \text{1. Plane polarized (after Polaroid): } E_x = E_0\cos(kz - \omega t), \quad E_y = 0 \\ \text{2. Circularly polarized (QWP at } \phi = 45^\circ\text{): } E_x = \frac{E_0}{\sqrt{2}}\sin\omega t,\; E_y = \frac{E_0}{\sqrt{2}}\cos\omega t \implies E_x^2 + E_y^2 = \frac{E_0^2}{2} \\ \text{3. Elliptically polarized (QWP at } \phi \neq 45^\circ\text{): } \frac{E_x^2}{(E_0\sin\phi)^2} + \frac{E_y^2}{(E_0\cos\phi)^2} = 1
cards.body: Describe how a Polaroid/Nicol prism produces plane polarized light, and how a QWP at 45 degrees or general angle \(\phi\) produces circular or elliptical polarization. Plane 1.5 · circular & elliptical 2.5.

cards.q: When linearly polarized light passes through a quarter-wave plate with its electric vector parallel to the optic axis (\( \phi = 0^\circ \)), the emergent beam is ____.
cards.why: At \(\phi = 0\) degrees only the extraordinary wave is excited, so the beam remains linearly polarized.

cards.q: In circularly polarized light, the two orthogonal electric field components have equal amplitudes and a phase difference of ____.
cards.why: Equal amplitudes with a 90-degree phase shift trace a circle.

cards.q: A Nicol prism eliminates the ordinary ray by ____.
options: total internal reflection at a Canada balsam layer
cards.why: Since \(n_o (1.658) > n_{balsam} (1.55) > n_e (1.486)\), the o-ray is totally internally reflected.

sheets.title: Q25 · Mirror equation from Fermat's principle (4 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 4 marks
cards.title: Question 25
cards.q: Use Fermat's principle to determine the mirror equation for an object point at a distance less than \(R/2\) from a concave mirror of radius of curvature R.
Optical path expression L = OS + SI (or OS - SI for virtual image) and paraxial expansion

options.t: Path length expanded in small angle \(\theta\) (or height h) using cosine law / binomial theorem

cards.why: Expand the ray path OS and SI in powers of the small paraxial angle \(\theta\) (or height h).

cards.q: Stationary condition dL/\(d \theta = 0\) and sign convention yielding \(1/u + 1/v = 2/R\)

options.t: Derivative dL/\(d \theta = 0\) equated and mirror equation \(1/u + 1/v = 2/R\) obtained

cards.why: Differentiate the path length with respect to \(\theta\) and apply the sign convention to get \(1/u + 1/v = 2/R\).

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Mirror equation \(1/u + 1/v = 2/R\) from Fermat's principle
cards.body: Know first: Laws of reflection and refraction from Fermat's principle. For an axial object \( O \) at distance \( x < r/2 \) in front of a concave mirror of radius \( r \), the reflected ray appears to diverge from a virtual image \( I \) at distance \( y \) behind the pole \( P \). By Fermat's principle (Example 3.4), \( L = OS - SI \) is stationary for paraxial rays. Expanding in small angle \( \theta \) gives \( OS \approx x + \frac{1}{2}r^2\left(\frac{1}{x} - \frac{1}{r}\right)\theta^2 \) and \( SI \approx y + \frac{1}{2}r^2\left(\frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{r}\right)\theta^2 \). Setting \( \frac{dL}{d\theta} = 0 \) yields \( \frac{1}{x} - \frac{1}{y} = \frac{2}{r} \), which with \( u = -x, v = +y, R = -r \) becomes \( \frac{1}{u} + \frac{1}{v} = \frac{2}{R} \).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Fermat derivation of concave mirror equation
cards.tex: OS = \left[(r - x)^2 + r^2 + 2r(r - x)\cos\theta\right]^{1/2} \approx x + \frac{1}{2}r^2\left(\frac{1}{x} - \frac{1}{r}\right)\theta^2 \\ SI = \left[(r + y)^2 + r^2 - 2r(r + y)\cos\theta\right]^{1/2} \approx y + \frac{1}{2}r^2\left(\frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{r}\right)\theta^2 \\ L = OS - SI \approx (x - y) + \frac{1}{2}r^2\left(\frac{1}{x} - \frac{1}{y} - \frac{2}{r}\right)\theta^2 \\ \frac{dL}{d\theta} = 0 \implies \frac{1}{x} - \frac{1}{y} = \frac{2}{r} \\ \text{Sign convention } (u = -x,\; v = +y,\; R = -r): \quad -\frac{1}{u} - \frac{1}{v} = -\frac{2}{R} \implies \frac{1}{u} + \frac{1}{v} = \frac{2}{R}
cards.body: Expand OS and SI in powers of \(\theta^2\), apply dL/\(d \theta = 0\), and substitute the Cartesian signs \(u = -x\), \(v = +y\), \(R = -r\). Path expansion 2 · extremum & sign convention 2.

cards.label: Derivation
cards.title: Mirror equation from Fermat's principle, step by step
cards.legend: Object \(O\) at distance \(x\) from the concave mirror pole \(P\) (centre \(C\)). The ray \(OSI\) reflects at height \(h\) on the mirror, and the image is at \(y\).

phases.name: Cosine-law segments
phases.why: write the path via the mirror point S

phases.name: Paraxial expansion
phases.why: keep the first order in h

phases.name: Stationary condition
phases.why: the path must not change with h

phases.name: Cartesian signs
phases.why: u and R are negative

steps.note: Total optical path from \(O\) to the mirror point \(S\) and on to the image.
Use the binomial expansion for small \(h\); the mirror sag is \(h^2/2R\).

ask.q: What small-angle approximation is used for \(\cos\theta\) in these triangles?
ask.why: The first two terms of the cosine series are enough at first order in the paraxial angle.

steps.note: Factor out \(h^2/2\) from the terms in \(h\).

ask.q: Which condition from Fermat's principle fixes the image position?
options: The path is stationary with respect to \(h\)
ask.why: Fermat's principle requires \(dL/dh = 0\), so the bracket of the \(h^2\) term must vanish.

steps.note: The bracket must vanish for every paraxial ray.

ask.q: Why must the object lie closer than \(R/2\) for a virtual image?
options: Then the image forms behind the mirror
ask.why: For \(x<R/2\) the rays diverge after reflection, so the image is virtual and behind the mirror.

steps.note: With Cartesian signs the mirror equation keeps this form.

ask.q: Why are \(u\) and \(R\) negative in this concave mirror setup?
options: Cartesian convention: left of the pole
ask.why: Distances measured to the left of the pole are negative.

cards.q: When an object is placed between the pole and focus (\( |u| < |R|/2 \)) of a concave mirror, the image distance \( v \) is ____.
For a virtual image formed by reflection or refraction, Fermat's extremum condition applies to the quantity ____.
cards.why: As shown in Example 3.4 of Ghatak, for diverging rays the virtual path difference OS - SI is stationary.

cards.q: If an object is placed at the center of curvature (\( u = R \)) of a concave mirror, the image is formed at ____.

sheets.title: Q26 · Radii of 9th and 10th bright Newton's rings (4 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 4 marks
cards.title: Question 26
cards.q: In the Newton rings arrangement, the radius of curvature of the curved side of the planoconvex lens is 100cm. For \(\lambda = 6 \times 10^{-5}\)cm, what will be the radii of the 9th and 10th bright rings?
Bright ring radius formula \(r_n = \sqrt{(2n - 1) \lambda R / 2}\) and numerical values for \(n = 9\) and \(n = 10\)

options.t: \(r9 = 0.2258\) cm and \(r10 = 0.2387\) cm (or using \((2n+1)/2\): 0.2387 cm and 0.2510 cm) calculated
Used dark ring formula \(\sqrt{n \lambda R}\), giving 0.2324 cm and 0.2449 cm

cards.why: Use \(r_n = \sqrt{(2n - 1) \lambda R / 2}\) with \(R = 100\) cm and \(\lambda = 6\times 10^{-5}\) cm for \(n = 9\) and \(n = 10\).

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: \(r_9 = 0.2258\) cm and \(r_{10} = 0.2387\) cm
cards.body: Know first: Colours of thin films, Newton's rings, Michelson interferometer (11). The radius of the \( n \)-th bright Newton's ring in reflected light (air film, \( \mu = 1 \)) is \( r_n = \sqrt{\frac{(2n - 1)\lambda R}{2}} \). With \( R = 100\text{ cm} \) and \( \lambda = 6\times 10^{-5}\text{ cm} \): for \( n = 9 \), \( r_9 = \sqrt{8.5 \times 6\times 10^{-3}} = \sqrt{0.051} = 0.2258\text{ cm} \); for \( n = 10 \), \( r_{10} = \sqrt{9.5 \times 6\times 10^{-3}} = \sqrt{0.057} = 0.2387\text{ cm} \).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Calculation of \(r_9\) and \(r_{10}\) for bright rings
cards.tex: R = 100\text{ cm}, \quad \lambda = 6 \times 10^{-5}\text{ cm}, \quad \lambda R = 6 \times 10^{-3}\text{ cm}^2 \\ r_n = \sqrt{\frac{(2n - 1)\lambda R}{2}} \\ n = 9: \quad r_9 = \sqrt{\frac{17 \times 6 \times 10^{-3}}{2}} = \sqrt{0.051} = 0.2258\text{ cm} \\ n = 10: \quad r_{10} = \sqrt{\frac{19 \times 6 \times 10^{-3}}{2}} = \sqrt{0.057} = 0.2387\text{ cm}
cards.body: Substitute \(n = 9\) and \(n = 10\) into the reflected bright-ring radius formula. Formula 1 · \(r_9\) calculation 1.5 · \(r_{10}\) calculation 1.5.

cards.q: In reflected light, the radius of the \( n \)-th bright Newton's ring is proportional to the square root of ____.
cards.why: \(2t = (2n - 1) \lambda / 2\) gives \(r_n = \sqrt{(2n - 1) \lambda R / 2}\).

cards.q: The difference between the squares of the radii of two consecutive bright (or dark) rings \( r_{n+1}^2 - r_n^2 \) is ____.
cards.why: \(r_{n+1}^2 - r_n^2 = (n + 1/2)\lambda R - (n - 1/2)\lambda R = \lambda R\).

cards.q: If a plano-convex lens of larger radius of curvature \( R \) is used, the radii of the Newton's rings ____.
cards.why: Ring radius \(r_n\) is proportional to \(\sqrt{R}\).

sheets.title: Q27 · Linear separation between sodium D1 and D2 lines in focal plane (4 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 4 marks
cards.title: Question 27
cards.q: A grating (with 15,000 lines per inch) is illuminated by sodium light. The grating spectrum is observed on the focal plane of a convex lens of focal length 10cm. Calculate the separation between the D1 and D2 lines of sodium. The wavelengths of the \(D_1\) and \(D_2\) lines are 5890 and \(5896\AA\) respectively.
Grating element d, angular dispersion \(d \theta\), and linear separation dx = \(f d \theta\)

options.t: \(d = 2.54/15000 = 1.693\times 10^{-4}\) cm, \(\cos \theta1 = 0.937\), and linear separation dx = \(f d \theta = 3.78\times 10^{-3}\) cm (0.0378 mm)
Small-angle approximation dx = \(f d \lambda / d = 3.54\times 10^{-3}\) cm used

cards.why: Find grating spacing d, compute angular separation \(d \theta\) in first order, and multiply by focal length \(f = 10\) cm.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Linear separation dx = 0.0378 mm (3.78 x 10^-3 cm)
cards.body: Know first: N-slit Fraunhofer diffraction pattern and grating (14). With \( d = \frac{2.54\text{ cm}}{15000} = 1.693\times 10^{-4}\text{ cm} \) and \( m = 1 \), \( \sin\theta = \frac{\lambda}{d} = 0.348 \) so \( \cos\theta = 0.9375 \). For \( d\lambda = 6\text{ \AA} = 6\times 10^{-8}\text{ cm} \) and \( f = 10\text{ cm} \), the linear separation in the focal plane is \( dx = f\,d\theta = \frac{f\,m\,d\lambda}{d\cos\theta} = 3.78\times 10^{-3}\text{ cm} = 0.0378\text{ mm} \).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Calculation of focal-plane linear separation
cards.tex: d = \frac{2.54\text{ cm}}{15000} = 1.6933 \times 10^{-4}\text{ cm}, \quad f = 10\text{ cm}, \quad m = 1 \\ \lambda_1 = 5890\text{ \AA}, \quad \lambda_2 = 5896\text{ \AA}, \quad d\lambda = 6 \times 10^{-8}\text{ cm} \\ \sin\theta = \frac{5.893 \times 10^{-5}}{1.6933 \times 10^{-4}} = 0.3480 \implies \cos\theta = \sqrt{1 - 0.3480^2} = 0.9375 \\ \Delta\theta = \frac{m\,d\lambda}{d\cos\theta} = \frac{1 \times 6 \times 10^{-8}}{1.6933 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.9375} = 3.779 \times 10^{-4}\text{ rad} \\ \Delta x = f\Delta\theta = 10 \times 3.779 \times 10^{-4} = 3.78 \times 10^{-3}\text{ cm} = 0.0378\text{ mm}
cards.body: Calculate d in cm, evaluate \(d \theta = d \lambda / (d \cos \theta)\) in first order, and multiply by focal length \(f = 10\) cm. Grating spacing d 1 · angular separation 1.5 · linear separation dx 1.5.

cards.q: The linear dispersion \( dx / d\lambda \) in the focal plane of a lens of focal length \( f \) equals ____.
cards.why: Since dx = \(f d \theta\), linear dispersion is \(f (d \theta / d \lambda) = f m / (d \cos \theta)\).

cards.q: If a lens of twice the focal length \( f \) is used to focus the grating spectrum, the linear separation between the D1 and D2 lines ____.
cards.why: Linear separation dx = \(f \Delta \theta\) is directly proportional to f.

cards.q: In the grating equation \( d\sin\theta = m\lambda \), as the diffraction angle \( \theta \) increases, \( \cos\theta \) decreases and the angular dispersion ____.
cards.why: \(d \theta / d \lambda = m / (d \cos \theta)\) increases as \(\cos(\theta)\) decreases.

sheets.title: Q29 · Numerical aperture, acceptance angle, and cutoff wavelength of step-index fiber (4 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 4 marks
cards.title: Question 29
cards.q: Consider a step index fiber with \(n1 = 1.474\) and \(n2 = 1.470\) and having a core radius \(a = 4.5\mu m\). Determine the numerical aperture, acceptance angle and cutoff wavelength of the optical fiber?
Calculation of NA, acceptance angle \(\theta_a\), and cutoff wavelength \(\lambda_c\)

options.t: NA = 0.1085, \(\theta_a = 6.23\) deg, and \(\lambda_c = \dfrac{2\pi a\,\mathrm{NA}}{2.405} = 1.275\) um calculated
Two of the three quantities calculated correctly

cards.why: Use NA = \(\sqrt{n1^2 - n2^2}\), \(\theta_a = \sin^{-1}\)(NA), and single-mode cutoff \(V_c = 2.405 = 2 \pi a\) NA / \(\lambda_c\).

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: NA = 0.1085, \(\theta_a = 6.23\) deg, \(\lambda_c = 1.275\) um
cards.body: Know first: Laws of reflection and refraction from Fermat's principle. With \( n_1 = 1.474 \), \( n_2 = 1.470 \), and \( a = 4.5\text{ }\mu\text{m} \): (1) \( \text{NA} = \sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2} = \sqrt{0.011776} = 0.1085 \); (2) acceptance angle \( \theta_a = \sin^{-1}(0.1085) = 6.23^\circ \); and (3) single-mode cutoff wavelength (at \( V_c = 2.405 \)) is \( \lambda_c = \frac{2\pi a\,\text{NA}}{2.405} = 1.275\text{ }\mu\text{m} \) (\( 1275\text{ nm} \)).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Calculation of NA, \(\theta_a\), and cutoff wavelength
cards.body: Compute NA from n1 and n2, find \(\theta_a = \sin^{-1}\)(NA), and solve \(V_c = 2.405\) for the cutoff wavelength \(\lambda_c\). NA 1.5 · acceptance angle 1 · cutoff wavelength 1.5.

cards.q: The single-mode cutoff wavelength \( \lambda_c \) of a step-index fiber of core radius \( a \) is given by ____.
cards.why: Setting \(V = 2 \pi a\) NA / \(\lambda_c = 2.405\) gives \(\lambda_c = 2 \pi a\) NA / 2.405.

cards.q: A step-index fiber guides only a single mode when the operating wavelength \( \lambda \) is ____.
cards.why: \(V < 2.405\) requires \(\lambda > \lambda_c\).

cards.q: For a small core radius \( a = 4.5\text{ }\mu\text{m} \) and \( \text{NA} = 0.1085 \), the fiber at \( \lambda = 1.55\text{ }\mu\text{m} \) operates as a ____.
cards.why: Since 1.55 um > \(\lambda_c\) (1.275 um), \(V < 2.405\) and the fiber is single-mode.

sheets.title: Q30 · Radius of first half-period zone of a zone plate (4 marks)
sheets.source: PYQ Nov 2020 Q30 · also Nov 2018 Q26

cards.label: PYQ · 4 marks
cards.title: Question 30
cards.q: Find the radius of the first half period zone on a zone plate, behaving like a convex lens of focal length 60cm. Given \(\lambda\) as \(6000\AA\).
Formula \(r1 = \sqrt{f \lambda}\) and numerical value

options.t: Formula \(r1 = \sqrt{f \lambda}\) and \(r1 = 0.06\) cm (0.6 mm) with units

cards.why: Substitute \(f = 60\) cm and \(\lambda = 6\times 10^{-5}\) cm into \(r1 = \sqrt{f \lambda}\).

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: First zone radius \(r1 = 0.06\) cm (0.6 mm)
cards.body: Know first: Fresnel diffraction and zone plate (15). For a zone plate of principal focal length \( f = 60\text{ cm} \) and wavelength \( \lambda = 6000\text{ \AA} = 6\times 10^{-5}\text{ cm} \), the radius of the first half-period zone is \( r_1 = \sqrt{f\lambda} = \sqrt{60 \times 6\times 10^{-5}} = \sqrt{36\times 10^{-4}} = 0.06\text{ cm} = 0.6\text{ mm} \).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Calculation of first zone radius
cards.tex: f = 60\text{ cm}, \quad \lambda = 6000\text{ \AA} = 6 \times 10^{-5}\text{ cm} \\ r_1 = \sqrt{f\lambda} = \sqrt{60 \times 6 \times 10^{-5}} = \sqrt{36 \times 10^{-4}}\text{ cm} = 0.06\text{ cm} = 0.6\text{ mm}
cards.body: Convert \(\lambda = 6000\) A to \(6\times 10^{-5}\) cm and evaluate \(r1 = \sqrt{f \lambda}\). Formula 1.5 · substitution 1 · result with units 1.5.

cards.q: For \( f = 60\text{ cm} \) and \( \lambda = 6000\text{ \AA} \), the radius of the 6th zone \( r_6 = r_1\sqrt{6} \) is ____.
cards.why: \(r6 = \sqrt{6 f \lambda} = 0.06 \cdot \sqrt{6}\) cm = 0.147 cm (asked in Nov 2018 Q9).

cards.q: A zone plate brings parallel light to a bright focus primarily by ____.
cards.why: Exposed odd (or even) half-period zones send in-phase diffracted wavelets to the focus.

cards.q: If all the transparent and opaque zones of a zone plate are interchanged (phase reversal/negative plate), the focal length ____.
cards.why: Whether odd or even zones are open, the focal distance \(f = r1^2 / \lambda\) is identical.

sheets.title: Q31 · Wedge angle of a thin air wedge from fringe density (4 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 4 marks
cards.title: Question 31
cards.q: Two plane glass plates are placed on top of each other, and on one side a cardboard is introduced to form a thin wedge of air. Assuming that a beam of wavelength \(6000\AA\) is incident normally, and there are 100 interference fringes per centimeter, calculate the wedge angle.
Fringe width \(\beta = 1/100\) cm and wedge angle \(\theta = \lambda / (2 \beta)\)

options.t: Formula and substitution with minor unit slip

cards.why: 100 fringes per cm gives \(\beta = 0.01\) cm; substitute into \(\theta = \lambda / (2 \beta)\).

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Wedge angle \(\theta = 3\times 10^{-3}\) rad (0.172 degrees)
cards.body: Know first: Colours of thin films, Newton's rings, Michelson interferometer (11). Since there are \( 100\text{ fringes/cm} \), the fringe width is \( \beta = \frac{1}{100}\text{ cm} = 0.01\text{ cm} \). For a normal-incidence air wedge (\( n = 1 \)) with \( \lambda = 6000\text{ \AA} = 6\times 10^{-5}\text{ cm} \), \( \beta = \frac{\lambda}{2\theta} \), giving \( \theta = \frac{\lambda}{2\beta} = \frac{6\times 10^{-5}}{2 \times 0.01} = 3\times 10^{-3}\text{ rad} = 0.172^\circ \).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Wedge angle calculation
cards.body: Find fringe width \(\beta = 0.01\) cm from the fringe density and apply \(\theta = \lambda / (2 \beta)\). Fringe width \(\beta 1.5\) · formula 1 · wedge angle \(\theta 1.5\).

cards.q: In an air wedge of angle \( \theta \), if the wedge angle is doubled, the number of fringes per centimeter ____.
cards.why: Fringe width \(\beta = \lambda / (2 \theta)\) halves, so the number of fringes per cm \((1/\beta)\) doubles.

cards.q: At the line of contact (apex) of two clean glass plates forming an air wedge, the zero-order reflected fringe is ____.
cards.why: At \(t = 0\), the \(\pi\) phase change upon reflection at the lower glass plate produces a straight dark fringe.

cards.q: If a wire of diameter \( d \) is placed at distance \( L \) from the apex of an air wedge, the wedge angle \( \theta \) in radians is ____.
cards.why: For small angles, \(\tan(\theta)\) ~ \(\theta = d / L\).

sheets.title: Q32 · Michelson interferometer: standardization of meter and circular, straight, white-light fringes (10 marks)
sheets.source: PYQ Nov 2020 Q32 · also Nov 2019 Q21

cards.label: PYQ · 10 marks
cards.title: Question 32
cards.q: Describe Michelson interferometer and explain how it is used to standardize the meter. Explain how circular, straight and white light fringes are formed.
Description of Michelson interferometer and formation of circular, straight, and white-light fringes

options.t: Diagram/working and conditions for circular (M1 || M2'), straight/localized (M1 inclined to M2'), and white-light fringes (d = 0 with central dark achromatic fringe) explained
Setup and only one or two fringe types explained

cards.why: Describe the interferometer and explain how mirror alignment and path difference produce circular, straight, and white-light fringes.

cards.q: Standardization of the meter using cadmium red wavelength and etalons

options.t: Counting fringes \(N = 2d/\lambda\) using stepped etalons and cadmium red line (6438.4696 A) to express 1 meter in wavelengths explained

cards.why: Explain how Michelson used stepped etalons and white-light zero-path reference to count wavelengths in the standard meter.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Michelson interferometer fringe types and standardization of the meter
cards.body: Know first: Colours of thin films, Newton's rings, Michelson interferometer (11). In a Michelson interferometer: (1) Circular Haidinger fringes of equal inclination (\( 2d\cos\theta + \lambda/2 = m\lambda \)) form when \( M_1 \) is strictly parallel to the virtual image \( M_2' \) (\( d \neq 0 \)); (2) Straight (or curved) Fizeau fringes of equal thickness form when \( M_1 \) and \( M_2' \) are slightly inclined, enclosing a wedge-shaped air film; (3) White-light fringes form when \( M_1 \) intersects \( M_2' \) (\( d = 0 \)), giving a central dark achromatic fringe flanked by 8–10 coloured fringes. Standardization of the meter: Using the monochromatic red cadmium line (\( \lambda = 6438.4696\text{ \AA} \)) and nine stepped Fabry-Perot/Michelson etalons (each double the previous length, aligned via white-light fringes), Michelson counted \( N = 2L/\lambda \) fringes and found \( 1\text{ m} = 1,553,163.5\,\lambda_{\text{Cd}} \).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Fringe conditions and meter standardization
cards.tex: \text{1. Circular fringes } (M_1 \parallel M_2'): \quad 2d\cos\theta + \frac{\lambda}{2} = m\lambda \\ \text{2. Straight wedge fringes } (M_1 \text{ inclined at } \alpha \text{ to } M_2'): \quad 2x\alpha + \frac{\lambda}{2} = m\lambda \\ \text{3. White-light fringes } (d = 0): \quad \Delta = \frac{\lambda}{2} \text{ for all } \lambda \text{ at center (dark central fringe)} \\ \text{4. Meter standardization: } L = \frac{N\lambda}{2} \implies 1\text{ m} = 1,553,163.5\,\lambda_{\text{Cd}} \; (\lambda_{\text{Cd}} = 6438.4696\text{ \AA})
cards.body: Describe the interferometer, explain the geometry of M1 and M2' for circular, straight, and white-light fringes, and outline the etalon comparison method for the standard meter. Apparatus & 3 fringe types 6 · meter standardization 4.

cards.q: In a Michelson interferometer, straight localized fringes are observed when mirror \( M_1 \) and virtual image \( M_2' \) are ____.
options: slightly inclined to form a thin air wedge
cards.why: Tilting one mirror creates a wedge-shaped air film that forms straight fringes of equal thickness.

cards.q: With white light in a Michelson interferometer (with compensating plate), the central fringe at \( d = 0 \) is ____.
cards.why: At \(d = 0\), the sole phase difference is \(\pi\) from internal vs external reflection at G1.

cards.q: Why are white-light fringes crucial in Michelson's standardization of the meter?
options: They accurately locate the position of zero path difference (coincidence of mirrors)
They have the longest coherence length
cards.why: Only the zero-order fringe is achromatic in white light, allowing exact coplanar alignment of etalon mirrors.

sheets.title: Q33 · Fraunhofer diffraction due to a single narrow slit (10 marks)
sheets.source: PYQ Nov 2020 Q33 · also Nov 2022 (D 30197) Q33, Nov 2021 (CBCSS) Q21, Nov 2019 Q33, Nov 2018 Q32

cards.label: PYQ · 10 marks
cards.title: Question 33
cards.q: Discuss Fraunhofer type of diffraction produced by a narrow slit illuminated by monochromatic light. Obtain the positions of the maxima and minima and draw a diagram to indicate the distribution intensity of light in the diffraction pattern.
Ray diagram and derivation of single-slit intensity \(I = I0 (\sin \beta / \beta)^2\)

options.t: Setup diagram and complete integration/phasor derivation of \(I = I0 (\sin \beta / \beta)^2\) with \(\beta = \pi b \sin \theta / \lambda\)
Formula stated with qualitative explanation only

cards.why: Derive the resultant amplitude \(A0 (\sin \beta / \beta)\) by integrating secondary wavelets across the slit width b.

cards.q: Positions of central maximum, minima, secondary maxima, and intensity distribution curve

options.t: Central maximum \((\theta = 0)\), minima \((b \sin \theta = m \lambda)\), secondary maxima (\(\tan\beta = \beta\), \(\beta \approx (2m+1)\pi/2\)), and labelled intensity graph drawn
Minima stated without secondary maxima or graph

cards.why: Find the conditions for minima and secondary maxima and draw the sinc-squared intensity graph.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Single-slit Fraunhofer diffraction intensity and extrema
cards.body: Know first: Single-slit Fraunhofer diffraction pattern (12). When a plane wavefront of wavelength \( \lambda \) is diffracted at angle \( \theta \) by a slit of width \( b \), integrating the secondary wavelets across the slit gives the intensity \( I = I_0 \left(\frac{\sin\beta}{\beta}\right)^2 \), where \( \beta = \frac{\pi b\sin\theta}{\lambda} \). The central principal maximum occurs at \( \theta = 0 \) (\( I = I_0 \)). Minima of zero intensity occur when \( \beta = m\pi \) (\( b\sin\theta = m\lambda, \; m = \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots \)). Secondary maxima occur where \( \frac{dI}{d\beta} = 0 \implies \tan\beta = \beta \), approximately at \( \beta \approx \pm\frac{3\pi}{2}, \pm\frac{5\pi}{2}, \dots \) with relative intensities \( \frac{4}{9\pi^2}, \frac{4}{25\pi^2}, \dots \).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Derivation of single-slit amplitude, minima, and secondary maxima
cards.tex: dE = \frac{A_0}{b}dx\cos(\omega t - kx\sin\theta), \quad E = \frac{A_0}{b}\int_{-b/2}^{b/2}\cos(\omega t - kx\sin\theta)\,dx = A_0\frac{\sin\beta}{\beta}\cos\omega t \\ \beta = \frac{\pi b\sin\theta}{\lambda}, \quad I = I_0\left(\frac{\sin\beta}{\beta}\right)^2 \\ \text{1. Central maximum: } \beta \to 0 \implies \lim_{\beta\to 0}\frac{\sin\beta}{\beta} = 1 \implies I = I_0 \text{ at } \theta = 0 \\ \text{2. Minima } (I = 0): \quad \sin\beta = 0 \;(\beta \neq 0) \implies \beta = \pm m\pi \implies b\sin\theta = \pm m\lambda \; (m = 1, 2, 3, \dots) \\ \text{3. Secondary maxima: } \frac{dI}{d\beta} = 2I_0\frac{\sin\beta}{\beta}\frac{\beta\cos\beta - \sin\beta}{\beta^2} = 0 \implies \tan\beta = \beta \\ \beta \approx \pm\frac{3\pi}{2}, \pm\frac{5\pi}{2}, \dots \implies I_1 = \frac{4}{9\pi^2}I_0 \approx \frac{I_0}{22.2}, \quad I_2 = \frac{4}{25\pi^2}I_0 \approx \frac{I_0}{61.7}
cards.body: Integrate the secondary wavelets over [-b/2, b/2] to obtain \(I = I0 (\sin \beta / \beta)^2\), solve for zeros and extrema, and sketch the intensity distribution. Intensity derivation 5 · minima, maxima & graph 5.

cards.label: Derivation
cards.title: Single-slit Fraunhofer intensity, step by step
cards.legend: Slit \(AB\) of width \(b\) diffracts parallel rays at angle \(\theta\) to the point \(P\) on the screen. \(\beta = \pi b\sin\theta/\lambda\) is the half phase difference.

phases.name: Wavelet integration
phases.why: add the secondary wavelets across the slit

phases.name: Intensity law
phases.why: square the amplitude

phases.name: Minima condition
phases.why: the zeros of sin beta

phases.name: Secondary maxima
phases.why: differentiate I with respect to beta

steps.note: Each point of the slit emits a secondary wavelet; integrate across the width \(b\).

ask.q: What is the phase difference between the extreme rays from the two edges of the slit?
ask.why: The edge-to-edge path difference is \(b\sin\theta\), giving a phase difference of \(2\beta\).

steps.note: The integral gives \(\sin\beta/\beta\), with \(\beta = \pi b \sin\theta/\lambda\).

ask.q: What is the intensity law for the diffraction pattern?
ask.why: Intensity is the square of the amplitude \(E_\theta\).

steps.note: Square the amplitude; \(I_0\) is the central maximum intensity.

ask.q: Why is \(m = 0\) excluded from the minima condition \(b\sin\theta = m\lambda\)?
options: It is the edge of the slit
ask.why: At \(\theta = 0\), \(\beta = 0\) and the intensity is a maximum, not a minimum.

steps.note: Zeros of \(\sin\beta\) give the dark fringes for \(m = \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots\).
Setting \(dI/d\beta = 0\) between minima gives this transcendental equation; the first secondary maximum is near \(\beta \approx 1.43\pi\).

ask.q: How does the central maximum width compare with any secondary maximum?
options: Central maximum is twice as wide
ask.why: The central lobe runs between the first two minima, so it is about twice the width of a side lobe.

cards.q: In single-slit Fraunhofer diffraction, the linear width of the central maximum on a screen at focal distance \( f \) is ____.
cards.why: The first minima lie at +- \(f \lambda / b\) on either side of the center, giving total width \(2 f \lambda / b\).

cards.q: The ratio of the intensity of the first secondary maximum to that of the central principal maximum in a single-slit pattern is approximately ____.
If the width \( b \) of a single slit is narrowed, the central diffraction maximum on the screen becomes ____.
cards.why: Angular spread \(2 \theta1 = 2 \lambda / b\) is inversely proportional to slit width b.

sheets.title: Q34 · Plane, circular, and elliptical polarization; reflection/refraction polarization; circular production & detection (10 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 10 marks
cards.title: Question 34
cards.q: Distinguish between (1) plane (2) circular and (3) elliptical polarization. Discuss the production of linearly polarized light by reflection and refraction. How would you produce and detect circularly polarized light?
Distinction between plane, circular, and elliptical polarization

options.t: Locus of E-vector tip, amplitude equality, and phase difference (\(0/\pi\) vs \(\pi/2\) with equal amplitudes vs \(\pi/2\) or general \(\delta\) with unequal amplitudes) explained

cards.why: Contrast the trajectory of the electric vector and the phase/amplitude conditions for the three states.

cards.q: Production of linearly polarized light by reflection (Brewster's law) and refraction (pile of plates)

options.t: Brewster reflection \((\tan \theta_p = n)\) and refraction through a pile of plates at Brewster's angle explained with diagrams
Only reflection or only refraction explained

cards.why: Explain Brewster reflection (s-polarized reflected ray) and multiple refractions in a pile of plates (p-polarized transmitted ray).

cards.q: Production and detection of circularly polarized light

options.t: Production via QWP at 45 deg and detection using rotating analyzer + QWP (to distinguish from unpolarized light) explained
Only production explained without distinguishing circular from unpolarized light

cards.why: Explain how a QWP produces circular polarization and how a QWP + rotating analyzer distinguishes it from unpolarized light.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: States of polarization, reflection/refraction methods, and circular polarization analysis
cards.body: Know first: Production and analysis of polarised light (22). (1) In plane polarization, the electric vector \( \mathbf{E} \) oscillates along a fixed straight line (\( \delta = 0 \) or \( \pi \)); in circular polarization, \( \mathbf{E} \) has constant magnitude and rotates in a circle (\( E_{0x} = E_{0y}, \delta = \pm\pi/2 \)); in elliptical polarization, both magnitude and direction of \( \mathbf{E} \) vary as its tip traces an ellipse (\( E_{0x} \neq E_{0y} \) or general \( \delta \)). (2) By reflection at Brewster's angle \( \theta_p = \tan^{-1}n \), the reflected beam is completely s-polarized; by repeated refraction through a pile of glass plates inclined at \( \theta_p \), the s-component is progressively reflected away and the transmitted beam becomes nearly 100% p-polarized. (3) Circularly polarized light is produced by passing linearly polarized light through a QWP at \( 45^\circ \). To detect it, rotating an analyzer alone gives constant intensity (like unpolarized light); inserting a QWP before the rotating analyzer converts circularly polarized light into linearly polarized light, producing two complete extinctions per revolution.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Equations for polarization states and Brewster angle
cards.tex: \frac{E_x^2}{a^2} + \frac{E_y^2}{b^2} - \frac{2E_x E_y}{ab}\cos\delta = \sin^2\delta \implies \begin{cases} \delta = 0, \pi \to \text{Plane (line)} \\ a = b,\; \delta = \pm\frac{\pi}{2} \to \text{Circular} \\ a \neq b,\; \delta = \pm\frac{\pi}{2} \to \text{Elliptical} \end{cases} \\ \text{Reflection (Brewster): } \tan\theta_p = \frac{n_2}{n_1}, \quad \theta_p + r = 90^\circ \\ \text{Detection of CP: } \text{Rotating analyzer } (I = \text{const}) + \text{QWP } \to \text{LP } (I = I_0\cos^2\theta \text{ with zero minima})
cards.body: Compare the three states of polarization, explain Brewster reflection and pile-of-plates refraction, and detail the QWP + analyzer procedure for producing and detecting circular polarization. Three states 3.5 · reflection & refraction 3.5 · CP production & detection 3.

cards.q: In a pile-of-plates polarizer set at Brewster's angle, the transmitted light is linearly polarized with its electric vector ____.
options: perpendicular to the plane of incidence (s-polarized)
cards.why: At Brewster's angle, p-polarized light is 100% transmitted at every surface while s-polarized light is reflected off.

cards.q: When a beam of light is examined through a rotating Polaroid alone and shows no variation in intensity, the beam may be ____.
cards.why: Both unpolarized and circularly polarized light have equal time-averaged components in all transverse directions.

cards.q: To distinguish circularly polarized light from unpolarized light, one places a ____.
options: quarter-wave plate before the rotating analyzer
cards.why: A QWP converts circularly polarized light into linearly polarized light (giving extinction), whereas unpolarized light remains unpolarized.

sheets.title: Q1 · Determinant of translation matrix (1 mark)

cards.label: PYQ · 1 mark
cards.title: Question 1
cards.q: The determinant of translation matrix is ——————.
Value of determinant
cards.why: For T = \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ d/n & 1 \end{pmatrix}\), det\((T) = 1\cdot1 - 0\cdot(d/n) = 1\).

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: 1 (unity)
cards.body: Know first: Refraction and reflection at a single spherical surface. The determinant of the translation matrix \( \mathcal{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ d/n & 1 \end{bmatrix} \) is always equal to \( 1 \).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Determinant evaluation
cards.body: State 1. Answer 1.

cards.q: The determinant of any paraxial translation or refraction matrix using optical direction cosines is ____.
cards.why: Optical phase-space area (Lagrange-Helmholtz invariant) is conserved, making det\((M) = 1\).

cards.q: In the translation matrix \( \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ d/n & 1 \end{bmatrix} \), the upper-right element is ____.
cards.why: Because \(\lambda2 = \lambda1 + 0\cdoty1\), the (1,2) entry is zero.

cards.q: When two matrices of determinant 1 are multiplied together, the determinant of their product is ____.
cards.why: det(AB) = det(A) * det\((B) = 1 \cdot 1 = 1\).

sheets.title: Q4 · Recording several images in a single medium (1 mark)

cards.label: PYQ · 1 mark
cards.title: Question 4
cards.q: Several images can be recorded in a ——————.
Word filling the blank
cards.why: Several independent images can be recorded on a single hologram by changing the reference beam angle or wavelength.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Hologram
cards.body: Know first: Interference of light waves. Several independent images can be recorded on a single hologram (by varying the angle of incidence or wavelength of the reference wave).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Multiplexed hologram
cards.body: State 'hologram'. Answer 1.

cards.q: Recording multiple images on a single holographic plate at different reference angles is called ____.
cards.why: Each reference angle reconstructs its own corresponding object wave.

cards.q: Thick three-dimensional holograms that reconstruct only at the Bragg angle are called ____.
cards.why: Volume holograms store fringes throughout the thickness of the emulsion or crystal.

cards.q: In a hologram, the recorded pattern consists of microscopic ____.
cards.why: The hologram is a record of the interference fringes between reference and object beams.

sheets.title: Q5 · Change in optical path with refractive index of thin film (1 mark)

cards.label: PYQ · 1 mark
cards.title: Question 5
cards.q: The optical path traversed by light wave when reflected from the lower surface of a thin film —————— with increase of refractive index of the film
Effect of increasing refractive index
cards.why: Optical path in the film is \(2 n d \cos r = 2 d \sqrt{n^2 - \sin^2 i}\), which increases as n increases.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Increases
cards.body: Know first: Interference by division of amplitude and non-reflecting films (10). The optical path difference \( \Delta = 2nd\cos r = 2d\sqrt{n^2 - \sin^2 i} \) traversed by a light wave reflected from the lower surface of a thin film increases with an increase in the refractive index \( n \) of the film.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Dependence of 2nd \(\cos r\) on n
cards.tex: L_{\text{op}} = \frac{2nd}{\cos r}, \quad \Delta = 2nd\cos r = 2d\sqrt{n^2 - \sin^2 i} \quad (\text{increases with } n)
cards.body: State 'increases'. Answer 1.

cards.q: At normal incidence (\( i = 0 \)), the optical path traversed inside a film of thickness \( d \) and index \( n \) is ____.
cards.why: The wave travels down and back through thickness d, covering geometric distance 2d and optical path 2nd.

cards.q: In terms of the angle of incidence \( i \) in air, \( 2nd\cos r \) can be written as ____.
cards.why: Since \(n \cos(r) = \sqrt{n^2 - n^2 \sin^2 r} = \sqrt{n^2 - \sin^2 i}\), 2nd \(\cos(r) = 2d \sqrt{n^2 - \sin^2 i}\).

cards.q: As the angle of incidence \( i \) increases from \( 0^\circ \), the path difference \( 2nd\cos r \) in a thin film ____.
cards.why: Increasing i increases r, which decreases \(\cos(r)\).

sheets.title: Q7 · Circular aperture diffraction pattern shape (1 mark)

cards.label: PYQ · 1 mark
cards.title: Question 7
cards.q: Write True or False : The diffraction pattern due to circular aperture for a plane wave are concentric circular rings.
True/False identification
cards.why: By circular symmetry, Fraunhofer and Fresnel diffraction patterns of a circular aperture consist of concentric circular rings around a central disc/spot.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: True
cards.body: Know first: Single-slit Fraunhofer diffraction pattern (12). The statement is True. Because a circular aperture has axial symmetry, the diffraction pattern produced by a normally incident plane wave consists of a central disc surrounded by concentric alternating dark and bright circular rings.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Azimuthal symmetry of circular aperture
cards.body: State True. Answer 1.

cards.q: The diffraction pattern of a circular aperture consists of a central bright Airy disc surrounded by ____.
options: concentric dark and bright circular rings
cards.why: Axial symmetry produces concentric rings.

cards.q: Compared to the central Airy disc, the surrounding bright rings in circular aperture diffraction are ____.
cards.why: The first bright ring has peak intensity only 1.75% of the central maximum.

cards.q: In Fresnel diffraction by a circular aperture, as the screen distance is varied along the axis, the center of the pattern is ____.
cards.why: Depending on whether the aperture exposes an odd or even number of Fresnel half-period zones, the center is bright or dark.

sheets.title: Q8 · Polarization of ordinary and extraordinary rays (1 mark)

cards.label: PYQ · 1 mark
cards.title: Question 8
cards.q: Write True or False : Both Ordinary ray and Extra ordinary rays are plane polarized.
True/False identification
cards.why: Both the ordinary ray and the extraordinary ray are linearly (plane) polarized in mutually perpendicular planes.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: True
cards.body: Know first: Double refraction and Huygens' explanation (20). The statement is True. Both the ordinary ray (o-ray) and the extraordinary ray (e-ray) produced by double refraction are completely plane (linearly) polarized, with their vibrations perpendicular and parallel to the principal section of the crystal respectively.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Orthogonal linear polarizations of o-ray and e-ray
cards.body: State True. Answer 1.

cards.q: The vibrations of the ordinary ray in a doubly refracting crystal are always ____.
options: perpendicular to the principal section (optic axis plane)
cards.why: As shown in Eq. (22.43) of Ghatak, \(D_o\) is perpendicular to both k and the optic axis.

cards.q: The vibrations of the extraordinary ray lie ____.
options: in the principal section containing the ray and optic axis
cards.why: \(D_e\) lies in the plane containing k and the optic axis.

cards.q: The angle between the planes of vibration of the o-ray and e-ray emerging from a calcite crystal is ____.
cards.why: The two linearly polarized rays are orthogonally polarized.

sheets.title: Q9 · Effect of grating element on angular dispersion (1 mark)

cards.label: PYQ · 1 mark
cards.title: Question 9
cards.q: Write True or False : Larger the grating element larger will be the angular dispersion.
True/False identification
cards.why: Angular dispersion \(d \theta / d \lambda = m / (d \cos \theta)\) is inversely proportional to the grating element d.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: False
cards.body: Know first: N-slit Fraunhofer diffraction pattern and grating (14). The statement is False. The angular dispersion of a grating is \( \frac{d\theta}{d\lambda} = \frac{m}{d\cos\theta} \), which is inversely proportional to the grating element \( d = a + b \). Hence a smaller grating element (more lines per cm) gives larger angular dispersion.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Inverse dependence on grating element d
cards.body: State False because angular dispersion decreases when d increases. Answer 1.

cards.q: Angular dispersion of a diffraction grating is inversely proportional to the ____.
cards.why: \(d \theta / d \lambda = m / (d \cos \theta)\).

cards.q: To achieve high angular dispersion in a grating spectrometer, the number of ruled lines per centimeter should be ____.
cards.why: More lines per cm means a smaller grating element \(d = 1/N0\) and wider angular spread.

cards.q: Angular dispersion \( d\theta / d\lambda \) in order \( m \) is directly proportional to ____.
cards.why: Higher diffraction orders give greater angular dispersion.

sheets.title: Q10 · Hologram recording both intensity and phase (1 mark)

cards.label: PYQ · 1 mark
cards.title: Question 10
cards.q: Write True or False : A hologram records both intensity and phase of light wave.
True/False identification
cards.why: A hologram encodes both the amplitude (intensity) and phase of the object wave via interference with a reference beam.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: True
cards.body: Know first: Interference of light waves. The statement is True. By interfering the object wave with a coherent reference wave, a hologram records both the intensity (amplitude) and the phase distribution of the light wave.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Amplitude and phase encoding
cards.body: State True. Answer 1.

cards.q: In a hologram, the amplitude of the object wave is recorded as fringe contrast (visibility), while the phase is recorded as ____.
cards.why: Shifts in relative phase \(\phi_O - \phi_R\) shift the spatial positions of the interference maxima.

cards.q: Why does an ordinary photograph appear two-dimensional (flat)?
options: It records only intensity and loses all phase information
It has too high a resolution
cards.why: Without a reference beam, phase information is lost during square-law intensity detection.

cards.q: The 3D depth and parallax of a holographic image are direct results of reconstructing the original ____.
cards.why: Recreating the exact complex wavefront \(E_O\) makes the eye perceive the original 3D object.

sheets.title: Q11 · Fermat's principle of stationary time and elliptical reflector (2 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 11
cards.q: State Fermats principle of stationary time. Explain with respect to elliptical reflector.
Statement of Fermat's principle and constant path \(S1P + S2P\) in an elliptical reflector

options.t: Fermat's stationary-time principle stated and \(S1P + S2P\) = constant for all points P on an ellipse explained
Only Fermat's principle stated without elliptical reflector explanation

cards.why: State Fermat's principle and use the geometric property \(S1P + S2P\) = constant of an ellipse.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Fermat's principle and elliptical reflector
cards.body: Know first: Laws of reflection and refraction from Fermat's principle. Fermat's principle states that a light ray travelling between two points follows a path for which the optical path length (or transit time) is stationary with respect to nearby paths. For an elliptical reflector with foci \( S_1 \) and \( S_2 \) (Example 3.2), the sum of distances \( S_1P + S_2P \) is strictly constant for every point \( P \) on the ellipse; hence the transit time is stationary (neither maximum nor minimum, but constant) for all paths, and every ray emitted from focus \( S_1 \) reflects through the other focus \( S_2 \).
cards.tex: S_1 P + S_2 P = \text{constant} \implies \delta(S_1 P + S_2 P) = 0

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Stationary path in an ellipsoidal mirror
cards.tex: L_{\text{op}} = n(S_1 P + S_2 P) = 2na = \text{constant for all } P \text{ on ellipse} \\ \implies \delta L_{\text{op}} = 0 \text{ for every point } P
cards.body: State Fermat's principle and explain that \(S1P + S2P = 2a\) is constant for an ellipse, focusing all rays from S1 at S2. Principle 1 · elliptical reflector 1.

cards.q: For any point \( P \) on an elliptical mirror with foci \( S_1 \) and \( S_2 \), the path length \( S_1P + S_2P \) is ____.
cards.why: By definition of an ellipse, the sum of focal distances \(S1P + S2P = 2a\) is constant.

cards.q: In a pulsed ruby or Nd:YAG laser cavity, an elliptical cylindrical reflector is used so that all light from the flashlamp at one focus concentrates on the ____.
options: laser rod placed at the other focus
cards.why: As noted in Example 3.2 of Ghatak, an elliptical reflector efficiently couples flashlamp light into the laser rod.

cards.q: An elliptical reflector illustrates that Fermat's principle requires the transit time to be ____.
cards.why: All reflection paths from S1 to S2 via the ellipse take the exact same time.

sheets.title: Q12 · Selecting loudspeaker diameter for sound directionality (2 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 12
cards.q: To get more directionality for sound waves how will you select the diameter of the loud speaker ?
Relation \(\theta = 1.22 \lambda / D\) and selection of large diameter D

options.t: Select a larger diameter \(D (D >> \lambda)\) because angular divergence \(\theta = 1.22 \lambda / D\) is inversely proportional to D
States larger diameter without diffraction formula/reason

cards.why: Diffraction divergence \(\theta = 1.22 \lambda / D\) decreases as diameter D increases.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Choose a large diameter D compared to wavelength
cards.body: Know first: Single-slit Fraunhofer diffraction pattern (12). The angular divergence (half-angle spread) of waves emitted through a circular aperture of diameter \( D \) is \( \sin\theta_1 = \frac{1.22\lambda}{D} \). To obtain high directionality (small angular spread \( \theta_1 \)) for sound waves, the diameter \( D \) of the loudspeaker should be chosen as large as possible compared to the acoustic wavelength \( \lambda \).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Diffraction divergence of circular speaker
cards.body: Write the circular-aperture diffraction divergence formula and state that D must be large. Formula 1 · selection of large D 1.

cards.q: To minimize diffraction spreading and achieve a narrow, directional beam, the aperture diameter \( D \) must be ____.
cards.why: \(\theta = 1.22 \lambda / D\) is small only when \(D >> \lambda\).

cards.q: Audible sound waves bend around doorways much more noticeably than visible light because sound has a ____.
options: much longer wavelength comparable to the doorway width
cards.why: Diffraction is strong when \(\lambda / D\) is not small.

cards.q: For a loudspeaker of fixed diameter \( D \), high-frequency (short-wavelength) treble notes compared to low-frequency bass notes are ____.
cards.why: Smaller \(\lambda\) gives smaller divergence angle \(\theta = 1.22 \lambda / D\).

sheets.title: Q13 · Constructive and destructive interference conditions for normal incidence on a thin film (2 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 13
cards.q: For the normal incidence of a parallel light beam on a thin film of refractive index n, state the condition for destructive and constructive interference. Explain.
Conditions for constructive and destructive interference at normal incidence \((\cos r = 1)\) with explanation of \(\lambda/2\) phase shift

options.t: 2nd = \((2m-1)\lambda/2\) (constructive) and 2nd = \(m \lambda\) (destructive) in reflected light with \(\lambda/2\) reflection phase shift explained
Formulas stated without explaining the \(\lambda/2\) phase change

cards.why: At normal incidence \((\cos r = 1)\), include the \(\lambda/2\) reflection shift at the upper air-film surface.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Normal-incidence thin-film interference conditions
cards.body: Know first: Interference by division of amplitude and non-reflecting films (10). For normal incidence (\( i = r = 0, \cos r = 1 \)) on a film of thickness \( d \) and index \( n \) in air, the geometric path difference is \( 2nd \) and reflection at the denser top surface adds \( \lambda/2 \), so \( \Delta = 2nd + \lambda/2 \). Thus, in reflected light, constructive interference occurs when \( 2nd = (2m - 1)\frac{\lambda}{2} \) and destructive interference occurs when \( 2nd = m\lambda \) (and vice versa in transmitted light).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Reflected and transmitted normal-incidence conditions
cards.body: State the effective path difference 2nd + \(\lambda/2\) at normal incidence and write the constructive and destructive conditions. Conditions 1 · explanation 1.

cards.q: At normal incidence on a soap film in air, destructive interference in reflected light occurs when \( 2nd \) equals ____.
cards.why: 2nd + \(\lambda/2 = (2m+1)\lambda/2\) simplifies to 2nd = \(m \lambda\).

cards.q: At normal incidence on a thin film in air, constructive interference in transmitted light occurs when \( 2nd \) equals ____.
cards.why: In transmitted light the twice-reflected ray experiences two internal reflections (zero phase shift), so 2nd = \(m \lambda\) gives maxima.

cards.q: When a thin film of index \( n_2 \) is coated on a glass substrate of higher index \( n_3 > n_2 > n_1 \), a phase shift of \( \pi \) occurs at ____.
cards.why: Both reflections (air to film and film to glass) are at optically denser media.

sheets.title: Q14 · Explanation of colour of thin films (2 marks)
sheets.source: PYQ Nov 2019 Q14 · also Nov 2022 (CBCSS) Q4, Nov 2022 (D 30197) Q14, Nov 2021 (D 10245) Q14

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 14
cards.q: Explain colour of thin films.
White-light thin-film interference and wavelength dependence of 2nd \(\cos r\)

options.t: Interference of white light reflected from top and bottom surfaces, with 2nd \(\cos r\) satisfying constructive/destructive conditions for different wavelengths at different t and r
Mentions interference without explaining why different colours appear

cards.why: Explain how the path difference 2nd \(\cos r + \lambda/2\) reinforces certain wavelengths of white light and cancels others.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Origin of colours in thin films
cards.body: Know first: Colours of thin films, Newton's rings, Michelson interferometer (11). When a thin film (such as an oil slick or soap bubble) is illuminated by an extended white-light source, rays reflected from the upper and lower surfaces interfere with effective path difference \( \Delta = 2nd\cos r + \lambda/2 \). Because \( \Delta \) depends on wavelength \( \lambda \), thickness \( d \), and inclination \( r \), at any point and viewing angle some wavelengths satisfy destructive interference and are absent while others satisfy constructive interference, causing the film to display vivid varying colours.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Wavelength-selective interference condition
cards.body: Explain that white light contains all visible wavelengths and the interference condition selects different colours as thickness d and viewing angle r vary. Mechanism 1 · condition & variation 1.

cards.q: The colour seen at a particular point on a thin film changes when the observer moves their eye because the ____.
options: speed of light in vacuum changes
cards.why: Changing the viewing angle changes \(\cos(r)\) in 2nd \(\cos(r)\), shifting which wavelength is reinforced.

cards.q: If a thin film is illuminated by strictly monochromatic sodium light instead of white light, one observes ____.
cards.why: A single wavelength produces only bright (yellow) maxima and dark minima.

cards.q: At any point on a thin film, the colours seen in reflected light and transmitted light are ____.
cards.why: Wavelengths cancelled in reflection are strongly transmitted.

sheets.title: Q17 · Why interference colours are not observed in thick plates (2 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 2 marks
cards.title: Question 17
cards.q: Interference colours are not observed in thick plates or glass slabs. Why ?
Overlapping of many wavelengths satisfying 2nd \(\cos r = m \lambda\) and coherence length limit

options.t: Large path difference 2nd >> \(l_c\) (exceeds coherence length of white light) and many wavelengths simultaneously satisfy constructive interference, blending into uniform white
Only states path difference is large

cards.why: Explain that for large d, many visible wavelengths satisfy constructive interference simultaneously (and 2nd exceeds the white-light coherence length), producing uniform white illumination.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Why thick plates show uniform white instead of colours
cards.body: Know first: Colours of thin films, Newton's rings, Michelson interferometer (11). In a thick glass plate (\( d \gg \lambda \)), the path difference \( 2nd\cos r \) is very large: (1) it exceeds the short coherence length of white light (\( \sim\text{few }\mu\text{m} \)), and (2) at any point, a large number of closely spaced wavelengths across the entire visible spectrum simultaneously satisfy the constructive condition \( 2nd\cos r = (2m-1)\lambda/2 \) for high orders \( m \). Their superposition blends to give uniform white light to the eye.

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: High-order spectral overlap in a thick film
cards.tex: 2nd\cos r = (2m - 1)\frac{\lambda}{2} \implies \text{for large } d,\; \Delta\lambda \approx \frac{\lambda^2}{2nd} \ll \text{visible range} \\ \implies \text{many colours overlap at every point } \to \text{uniform white}
cards.body: Explain that in a thick slab many visible wavelengths simultaneously interfere constructively at high order m (and 2nd exceeds coherence length), mixing to white. Explanation 2.

cards.q: In a thick glass slab illuminated by white light, interference colours are absent because at every point ____.
options: many visible wavelengths satisfy constructive interference and mix to white
no light is reflected from the bottom surface
cards.why: Closely spaced maxima throughout the visible spectrum blend into white.

cards.q: The coherence length of ordinary white light is of the order of ____.
cards.why: Broad spectral width \(\Delta \lambda\) ~ 300 nm gives \(l_c = \lambda^2 / \Delta \lambda\) ~ \(1-2\) um.

cards.q: To observe Haidinger fringes in a relatively thick plane-parallel plate (such as a Fabry-Perot or Michelson plate), one must use ____.
cards.why: Monochromatic light has a long coherence length and avoids overlapping of multiple colours.

sheets.title: Q18 · Condition for image plane with respect to a refracting surface (4 marks)

cards.label: PYQ · 4 marks
cards.title: Question 18
cards.q: Derive the condition for image plane with respect to a refracting surface.
Paraxial refraction derivation or matrix derivation of \(n2/v - n1/u = (n2 - n1)/R\)

options.t: Complete derivation of Gaussian image plane condition \(n2/v - n1/u = (n2 - n1)/R\) (via paraxial geometry or object-to-image matrix)

cards.why: Derive the Gaussian equation \(n2/v - n1/u = (n2 - n1)/R\) relating the object distance u and image plane distance v.

cards.label: Answer
cards.title: Image plane condition for a single spherical refracting surface
cards.body: Know first: Refraction and reflection at a single spherical surface. For a spherical refracting surface of radius \( R \) separating media \( n_1 \) and \( n_2 \), paraxial Snell's law \( n_1\phi_1 = n_2\phi_2 \) with \( \phi_1 = \beta + \alpha_1 \approx \frac{h}{r} + \frac{h}{x} \) and \( \phi_2 = \beta - \alpha_2 \approx \frac{h}{r} - \frac{h}{y} \) (or setting \( M_{21} = 0 \) in the object-to-image matrix) gives the image plane condition \( \frac{n_2}{v} - \frac{n_1}{u} = \frac{n_2 - n_1}{R} \).

cards.label: Solution
cards.title: Derivation of Gaussian image condition
